target_corpus.text: Plain-language guidance for a general reader: the Federal plain language guides, the Google developer documentation style guide and the Microsoft Writing Style Guide, read as the register target and never as shippable text. Those guides use em dashes and semicolons in good writing, which is why most marks are counted here and never removed by the tool. The em dash in prose and the arrow inside a sentence are the two exceptions, and each gets a warn with an instruction to rewrite the sentence.

per_unit.question: Does the "+N" suffix name a count the text supports, or is it a chatbot's own citation-count marker?
per_unit.pass_line: the suffix names a count the text supports, so it weighs nothing
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the suffix is a citation-count marker and no citation is here
per_unit.generator: C011's own pattern hits, plus a "+N" suffix on a bare number

per_unit.question: Does the sentence carry a date or a source-availability claim the text supports, or is it the model's own guess?
per_unit.pass_line: a date protects the sentence, which is standard in journalism and research for time-sensitive data (9.B2)
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the phrase hedges a fact the draft never checked

per_unit.question: Does the entry carry the sense its qualifier names, for example "tapestry (figurative)" or "harness, not a test harness"?
per_unit.pass_line: the technical sense, so accurate domain vocabulary is kept (10.A2)
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the figurative sense, so the word counts with the vocabulary set

per_unit.question: Does the connector state a relation that holds between the adjacent propositions?
per_unit.pass_line: the relation holds, and an ordinary transition can aid comprehension (T06, 2.A1)
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: nothing was being added to, so the connector states no relation

per_unit.question: Does "Look," stand alone and line-initial before a routine claim, or does it sit inside a casual sentence?
per_unit.pass_line: inside a casual sentence, which is ordinary (6.A3)
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: a standalone opener before a routine claim

per_unit.question: Does the signpost help a reader navigate, or does it only announce what the next sentence says?
per_unit.pass_line: recaps needed for teaching, accessibility or executive navigation may be useful (T03)
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the signpost announces the next sentence and carries nothing

per_unit.question: Does the sentence say what to do, or that something is generally done?
per_unit.pass_line: the sentence says what to do
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the opener hedges a generality and names no action

per_unit.question: Is the noun a term of art here, as "surface" is in "API surface" and "harness" is in "test harness", or is it a metaphor?
per_unit.pass_line: a term of art in this register, so it weighs nothing
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: an abstract metaphor where a concrete noun would do

per_unit.question: Is this debate framing, a low-importance preamble, or belaboring how much something is conserved, rather than a claim the text supports?
per_unit.pass_line: the framing names a real debate, a real cost or a real measurement
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: stock framing with nothing behind it

per_unit.question: Does the last unit end on a concrete sentence the draft already carries, or on a dramatic fragment, a restatement or a stock send-off?
per_unit.pass_line: the closer carries a concrete claim
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: delete it, then end on the clearest concrete sentence already in the draft (6.B2)

per_unit.question: does the unit carry two or more counted intensifiers?
per_unit.pass_line: a single intensifier, or one of "really", "just" or "actually", excluded for sense ambiguity
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: two or more counted intensifiers sit in one unit

per_unit.question: is the quantifier backed by a named, specific set the text supports, or is it a lazy extreme with nothing behind it?
per_unit.pass_line: a quantifier backed by a named set, judged on text evidence, passes
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: "every", "always", "never" or another lazy extreme names no real set

per_unit.question: does the text name the convention or cite where the fix is standard?
per_unit.pass_line: a named convention or a citation clears the flag
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: "the standard fix is...", "the common approach is..." or "simple enough on paper" names no convention or citation

per_unit.question: Three poisons: did anyone make the judgment the first half denies, are the two halves the same thing in two registers, does deleting the contrast lose nothing? Any yes fires. Question 1 on text evidence only, default FIRE
per_unit.pass_line: both halves name a system, a number or a source, or the negative half corrects a live misconception
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: any of the three poisons answers yes

per_unit.question: Three poisons: did anyone make the judgment the first half denies, are the two halves the same thing in two registers, does deleting the contrast lose nothing? Any yes fires.
per_unit.pass_line: each fragment names something the deleted contrast would lose
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the fragment triplet states nothing beyond its own pattern

per_unit.question: does the phrase argue against an unstated objection, and is the option one a reader would actually weigh?
per_unit.pass_line: an objection the text attributes or answers in full, or an option a reader would actually weigh
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: a phrase argues against an unstated objection with no option a reader would weigh

per_unit.question: "If it sounds like a pull-quote, rewrite it" (5.C8). "Would you say it out loud?" is the awkward-phrasing test, and an aphorism passes it
per_unit.pass_line: you would say it out loud, and it carries a real claim
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: an aphoristic phrase, template or figurative verb sounds profound and says little

per_unit.question: is the -ing rider, the copula-avoidance form, or the stand-in for "is", "was" or "began" attached to a claim or a named source with nothing behind it?
per_unit.pass_line: "the museum serves as both archive and gallery" is no tell on its own (clustering rule, 9.B5)
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: an -ing rider, a copula-avoidance form, or an elaborate stand-in carries no named source

per_unit.question: are the outlets named and what they said stated?
per_unit.pass_line: an already-defined expert group can be referenced (T06); a missing citation alone is not a tell
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: a vague attribution, a prestige-list form, or a canned notability phrase names no outlet and states nothing they said

per_unit.question: does the sentence use a named scaffolding shape, a setup sentence, a landing phrase, a participial reframe, a thesis-first opener, or one of the paired or chiasmus judgment shapes, to carry a real point, or only the shape?
per_unit.pass_line: the shape carries a real point of its own
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the shape carries nothing beyond its own template

per_unit.question: "If the point is clear, delete the aside." Is the span before the colon a complete clause? Does the colon replace a relation the sentence should state?
per_unit.pass_line: the colon precedes a list or an example
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: a mid-line colon, an interpretive-metadiscourse phrase, or a restatement opener stands in for the relation the sentence should state

per_unit.question: does an abstract noun act as the subject of an agentive verb, with no real actor named?
per_unit.pass_line: a person or a named system is the actor
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: an abstract noun takes an agentive verb with no real actor behind it

per_unit.question: does the vehicle share a property with the tenor? has the reader seen this comparison a hundred times?
per_unit.pass_line: the vehicle shares a real property with the tenor, and the comparison is not a cliche
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the vehicle shares no property with its tenor, or the comparison is one the reader has seen a hundred times

per_unit.question: does a question sentence get answered at once by a sentence that just repeats its key noun?
per_unit.pass_line: a FAQ or tutorial file, or "Why? Because" inside a docstring (5.A9)
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the question is answered at once by a sentence repeating its own key noun

per_unit.question: does "imagine", "say a", "suppose", "for instance, a customer might" or "picture a" introduce an invented case where a real one would do?
per_unit.pass_line: a hypothetical is the right form in a tutorial or a spec
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the professional draft invents an illustrative case with no real one behind it

per_unit.question: Is the actor unknown or genuinely unimportant here, or does the text support naming one?
per_unit.pass_line: the actor is unknown or genuinely doesn't matter, or the sentence simply describes a state
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the passive construction hides an actor the text can support naming

per_unit.question: Each retained item has a clear role; no quota for list length.
per_unit.pass_line: a triad of real items, each with a clear role, passes (9.B6)
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the triad fills a quota with a filler item that carries no role of its own

per_unit.question: do the five parallel bullets each carry a distinct point, or only the shared gerund-opening template?
per_unit.pass_line: the parallel bullets follow the document's own template and each one carries a point
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: five bullets each open on the same gerund and run to the same length, carrying only the template

per_unit.question: does every list item open on a bold label with nothing more than the label itself?
per_unit.pass_line: the bold lead-in ends in a period, names the item, and is followed by genuinely new detail (15.A4)
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: every list item opens on a bold label carrying no more than the label

per_unit.question: does the first sentence under the heading only restate it, or treat the heading as a proper-noun subject, before any real content?
per_unit.pass_line: a one-line lead after a heading is also a legitimate docs style
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the first sentence under the heading restates it, or treats the title as a proper-noun subject, before real content

per_unit.question: would prose read better? would one or two sentences carry this without loss?
per_unit.pass_line: the table's rows are not reducible to one or two sentences without losing real structure
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: a small table could be one or two sentences instead

per_unit.question: does the title or heading read as an imperative command or a slogan?
per_unit.pass_line: the title or heading states its subject plainly
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: a detector finds an imperative title or a slogan

per_unit.question: does the list mark every item, or does the mark carry information?
per_unit.pass_line: the mark carries information the list needs
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: a feature list marks every item with a checkmark, U+2713 or U+2714, carrying no information of its own

per_unit.question: Is the flagged word protected industry terminology the text relies on, for example "margin expansion" for investors, or is it one the plain-word dictionary replaces?
per_unit.pass_line: the word is protected industry terminology, for example "margin expansion" for investors (19.A5)
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the word is one the plain-word dictionary replaces, with no protected industry sense behind it

per_unit.question: does the comment state a property the code visibly has?
per_unit.pass_line: the code beside the comment shows the property, so it stands
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the comment asserts a guarantee the code does not show

per_unit.question: Does the text drop the articles a sentence needs, as in "Parser rejects bad date", or lean on an abbreviation the reader must decode?
per_unit.pass_line: the text reads as whole sentences a reader decodes unaided
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: write the sentence out with its articles and the abbreviation spelled out

per_unit.question: does the message name what changed, or does it assure the reader about process?
per_unit.pass_line: the message names what changed, so the phrase is detail
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the message assures the reader about process where it should name the change

per_unit.question: Does the label mark a warning the reader would otherwise miss, or does it only announce the sentence after it?
per_unit.pass_line: the label marks a warning the reader would otherwise miss
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the label only announces the sentence after it, so cut it

per_unit.question: Does the example show a use the signature and the prose leave unclear, or is it a template block every function carries?
per_unit.pass_line: the example shows a use the signature leaves unclear
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: a template example block, so cut it or keep the one line a reader needs

per_unit.question: Does the header name an author and a date that version control already records, with a description the module docstring should carry?
per_unit.pass_line: the header carries something version control does not
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the author and the date belong to version control, so cut them and move the description to the module docstring

per_unit.question: Do the body's bullets add what the subject leaves out, or do they restate it?
per_unit.pass_line: the bullets add what the subject leaves out
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the bullets restate the subject, so write the body as the reason for the change

per_unit.question: Does the abstraction fit the problem or the template? Does the comment say why or what? Is the defensive code at a boundary? Would a senior engineer on this codebase have written it this way?
per_unit.pass_line: a senior engineer on this codebase would have written it this way
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the abstraction, the comment or the defensive check is one a senior engineer here would not have written

per_unit.question: is the sentence addressed to the document's reader about the reader's decision, or to the requester about the writer's inputs?
per_unit.pass_line: the sentence narrows scope, corrects the request, explains an omission or helps a reader navigate reference material, or it links a source the reader can use to check a figure (19.A1)
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the sentence tells the requester about the writer's inputs, which helps no reader of the deliverable

per_unit.question: Does the qualifier in the speaker notes caveat a claim the slide body makes, so the slide presents that claim without its caveat?
per_unit.pass_line: the qualifier caveats nothing the slide body claims, or the body states the same caveat in other words
per_unit.fire_line: FIRE: the slide body presents a claim whose caveat sits in the speaker notes alone

per_document.question: Does a light verb plus a nominalization here hide a plain verb?
per_document.pass_line: the nominalization names a thing the sentence needs
per_document.fire_line: FIRE: write the plain verb

per_document.question: Does the sentence work without the "you can" opener?
per_document.pass_line: the opener carries a real permission or a real option
per_document.fire_line: FIRE: cut the opener and start on the verb

per_document.question: is this sentence addressed to the person who asked for the text?
per_document.pass_line: a how-to or a template for people addresses its reader in the same words (judgment decides)
per_document.fire_line: FIRE: a remark addressed to the person who asked for the text is left inside the delivered artifact

per_document.question: does the answer show an answer-shaped habit, such as an unrequested option list, defining known terms, blanket caveats, or refusal-style disagreement, rather than the requested content?
per_document.pass_line: the structure serves the request itself, not a reflexive answer template
per_document.fire_line: FIRE: an answer-shaped habit appears, such as "Here's how I'd think about it", an unrequested option list, defining known terms, "Important caveats" on every claim, or refusal-style disagreement

per_document.question: does metaphor or flourish stand in for a direct statement here?
per_document.pass_line: the sentence says what it means directly
per_document.fire_line: FIRE: metaphor and flourish stand in for a direct statement

per_document.question: Does it name anything specific?
per_document.pass_line: the declarative names something specific
per_document.fire_line: FIRE: the declarative names nothing specific

per_document.question: is the sentence wordy and indirect where a direct one would serve the same content?
per_document.pass_line: the sentence is direct, or its indirection carries real content
per_document.fire_line: FIRE: the sentence is wordy and indirect with no content the direct form would lose

per_document.question: does a coined or unexplained jargon label appear where the industry uses a plain, standard term?
per_document.pass_line: "margin expansion" and other standard industry terms stay protected
per_document.fire_line: FIRE: a coined or unexplained jargon label appears in the document

per_document.question: does the reader know their next action, and does each paragraph or slide perform a clear function? "can you swap paragraphs 2 and 4 without breaking it?"
per_document.pass_line: each paragraph or slide performs a clear function the reader can name
per_document.fire_line: FIRE: the reader cannot tell their next action, or a paragraph or slide performs no clear function

per_document.question: is a number, a name or a unit used two ways in this document?
per_document.pass_line: the same number, name and unit are used consistently throughout
per_document.fire_line: FIRE: numbers, names or units disagree across units of one document

per_document.question: What does it tell the reader to do or know? Could it sit unchanged in another project's docs?
per_document.pass_line: the sentence names the mechanism or a number the reader needs
per_document.fire_line: FIRE: the sentence tells the reader nothing to do or know, and could move unchanged to another project's docs

per_document.question: does the text weigh every side because the subject has sides, or by habit, and does it cover every angle because the reader needs each one?
per_document.pass_line: the balance the text strikes matches what the subject and the reader actually need
per_document.fire_line: FIRE: the text weighs every side by habit, or covers every angle the reader does not need

per_document.question: does terminology or tone drift across the deck for the same thing?
per_document.pass_line: a term the document defines is masked (1.B7); distinct terms with distinct meanings are not merged
per_document.fire_line: FIRE: terminology and tone drift per deck for the same underlying thing

per_document.question: does the written deliverable pad with filler sections, redundant summaries or boilerplate?
per_document.pass_line: the deliverable covers the substance at the length the task needs
per_document.fire_line: FIRE: the deliverable pads with filler sections, redundant summaries or boilerplate

per_document.question: does every section end on a neat takeaway, or does the same callout follow every section?
per_document.pass_line: a document built on a template or a fixed format carries the shape by design
per_document.fire_line: FIRE: every section ends on a neat takeaway, or the same callout follows every section

per_document.question: would prose read better? would one or two sentences carry this without loss?
per_document.pass_line: the bullets or the header carry real structure prose would lose
per_document.fire_line: FIRE: a bullet list of half-sentences under a heading, or a header over a two-sentence section, could be one or two sentences instead

per_document.question: does this heading say what is under it, or only name a category?
per_document.pass_line: the heading names the subject and the date, or otherwise says what is under it
per_document.fire_line: FIRE: a topic heading names a category and says nothing of what sits under it

per_document.question: does any sentence in this document carry a hedge whose claim pulls in the opposite direction?
per_document.pass_line: every hedge and its claim pull the same direction throughout the document
per_document.fire_line: FIRE: some sentence carries a hedge whose claim pulls in the opposite direction

per_document.question: Does any comment say what the line after it already says, where a reader needs why?
per_document.pass_line: every comment says why, or names what the next line cannot
per_document.fire_line: FIRE: a comment restates the line after it, so cut it or say why

per_document.question: Would the writer recognize the edited draft as their own voice?
per_document.pass_line: the draft reads as the writer's own
per_document.fire_line: FIRE: the draft's voice would not be recognized by the writer

quote-mask.wording: A double-quoted span carries whatever it carries, and the phrase inside it is a quoted example rather than the writer's own sentence.
quote-mask.pass_line: quoted material, recorded and weighing nothing

code-mask.wording: A backtick-delimited span is code, and code is not prose.
code-mask.pass_line: inline code, recorded and weighing nothing

url-mask.wording: A bare URL is an address, and its characters are not the writer's prose.
url-mask.pass_line: a URL, recorded and weighing nothing

markdown-table-pipe.wording: Every vertical bar on a recognised markdown table row is syntax, whether it separates cells or is an escaped literal bar written as cell content, and the exception covers the bar alone. A dash or any other mark inside a cell still fires.
markdown-table-pipe.pass_line: table syntax, so the bar weighs nothing

html-comment-mask.wording: An HTML comment, its opening marker, its body and its closing marker alike, is not prose, and the closing marker carries the same two characters C018's ascii-arrow entry matches on their own.
html-comment-mask.pass_line: an HTML comment, recorded and weighing nothing

entity-mask.wording: A named HTML entity, checked against the small set of names a markdown document actually uses in prose, or a decimal or hexadecimal one, which are always unambiguous, is notation, not prose, and its closing semicolon is punctuation the writer never chose. A named form outside that set is not a real entity and is left exactly as written.
entity-mask.pass_line: an HTML entity, recorded and weighing nothing

wiki-alias-mask.wording: The target half of a [[target|alias]] construct names where a wiki link goes, which is not the writer's own prose, and the bar that separates it from the alias is syntax. A bar is required, since the bar is what makes a bracket pair an Obsidian link with an alias. A construct written with no bar is not a wiki link with an alias at all, since double brackets with no bar are also an ordinary editorial-note convention in plenty of documents, and it is left completely untouched. The alias, when one is written, is the writer's own display text, the exact counterpart of link text, and still weighs.
wiki-alias-mask.pass_line: a wiki link's target, recorded and weighing nothing

link-target-mask.wording: The target inside a markdown link's ](...) and the address inside a bare <mailto:...> autolink are where the link goes, not the writer's own prose, unlike the link text, which C010's placeholder rule already reads.
link-target-mask.pass_line: a link target, recorded and weighing nothing

C079.wording: A document title and its section headings label without a flag, since a well-made reference document does the same.
C079.pass_line: a document title or a section heading, exempted under C079

C090.wording: Each rule's own exceptions text clears its flag under `general`, judged on text evidence, with the exception named in the pass line.
C090.pass_line: the rule's own named exception, with the text evidence that clears it

C091.wording: A hedge ("I think", "maybe", "to be honest") or an adverb carrying emphasis, uncertainty or contrast stays when it expresses real uncertainty with text evidence, or, under `mine` only, the writer's spoken rhythm.
C091.pass_line: a hedge or an adverb with real uncertainty, emphasis or contrast behind it, recorded and weighing nothing

markdown-table-mask.wording: Every markdown table row is blanked for the rules that name this mask, since a cell holds labels and values, where a dash or an arrow is notation.
markdown-table-mask.pass_line: a table row, where the mark is notation

block-quote-mask.wording: Every line that opens with a block quote marker is blanked for the rules that name this mask, since a quoted passage keeps its own author's punctuation.
block-quote-mask.pass_line: a quoted passage, kept as its author wrote it
